claim: Morphometric measurements such as cortical thickness and subcortical volumetry can be used as surrogate biomarkers of aging.
source: Morphometric measurements such as cortical thickness and subcortical volumetry can be used as surrogate biomarkers of aging (Salat et al., 2004; Walhovd et al., 2005; Coupé et al., 2017) and disease (Lerch et al., 2005; Desikan et al., 2009; Dickerson et al., 2009; Blanken et al., 2017) via conﬁrmed histopathological changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Salat et al., 2004; Walhovd et al., 2005; Coupé et al., 2017).

claim: Integrating neuroimaging tools with neuropathological assessments can enable neuropathological–neuroimaging correlations for studying neurodegenerative diseases.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Webster et al., 2021.

claim: Ante mortem MRI studies provide accurate and reliable morphometric data.
source: While ante mortem magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies provide accurate and reliable morphometric data, they are often unavailable or occur too long before death, impeding reliable histopathological correlation.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Ex vivo MRI enables high-resolution image acquisition free of subject motion and other physiological noise.

claim: Ex vivo MRI has disadvantages including tissue degradation due to bacteria and autolysis from death to initiation of tissue fixation.
source: However, ex vivo MRI also has disadvantages, including: tissue degradation due to bacteria and autolysis from death to initiation of tissue ﬁxation; cross-linking of proteins due to ﬁxation that dramatically changes MRI properties of the tissue; and image artifacts caused by magnetic susceptibility interfaces that do not occur in vivo (Shatil et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shatil et al., 2016.

claim: The authors propose a novel software suite that enables three-dimensional reconstruction and quantitative 3D morphometry of dissection photographs.
source: To this end, we propose a novel software suite that, for the ﬁrst time, enables three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction and quantitative 3D morphometry of dissection photographs, powered by modern machine learning techniques (Goodfellow et al., 2016) and 3D surface scanning (Salvi et al., 2004).

claim: The proposed tools enable volumetric analysis of brain structures from photographs.
source: Provided that the photographs satisfy some basic requirements (presence of a ruler or ﬁducial markers to estimate pixel sizes), our tools enable volumetric analysis of brain structures from the photographs, computationally guided dissection via automated segmentation, and accurate spatial mapping for neuropathological–neuroimaging correlation.
evidence: The claim describes capabilities of the proposed tools.

claim: The software suite includes three modules: preprocessing routines, joint image registration algorithm, and machine learning segmentation.
source: Our suite is freely available and includes three modules. The ﬁrst module is a set of preprocessing routines for the photographs that enables the correction of perspective and calibration of pixel sizes. The second module is a joint image registration algorithm that allows 3D reconstruction of the photographs using a 3D surface scan of the brain as a reference. This module can also use a probabilistic atlas as a reference for the reconstruction, thus circumventing the need for a surface scanner. This scan-free mode enables retrospective analysis of photographs without corresponding 3D scans, albeit with lower accuracy than if surface scanning was available. The third and ﬁnal modules use machine learning to provide a high-resolution 3D image segmentation of the reconstructed stack.
evidence: The claim describes the structure of the proposed software.

evidence: The claim describes planned future work.

source: Additional future analyses will include: correlating the segmentation-derived volumes with clinical scores, disease subtypes, and disease duration; using techniques like SynthSR (Iglesias et al., 2023) to improve the resolution of the reconstructed volumes; exploring nonlinear deformation models for the 3D reconstruction; fully automatizing tissue segmentation from the background using neural networks; and extending the tools to 3D analysis of histological sections.
evidence: The claim describes planned future work.

claim: The new tools will allow extraction of quantitative phenotypical information from dissection photographs and thus augmentation of histopathological analysis.
source: Our new tools will allow extraction of quantitative phenotypical information from these photographs – and thus augmentation of histopathological analysis.
evidence: The claim is an assertion about the impact of the tools.

claim: The new methodology is expected to play a crucial role in the discovery of new imaging markers to study neurodegenerative diseases.
source: We expect this new methodology to play a crucial role in the discovery of new imaging markers to study neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the future impact of the work.

claim: The MADRC dataset includes dissection photography of fixed tissue and companion surface scans for 76 cases.
source: Dissection photography of ﬁxed tissue and companion surface scans for 76 cases from the Massachusetts Alzheimer's Research Center (18 whole cerebrums and 58 hemispheres).
evidence: The claim describes the dataset composition.

claim: The MADRC dataset includes 18 whole cerebrums and 58 hemispheres.
source: Dissection photography of ﬁxed tissue and companion surface scans for 76 cases from the Massachusetts Alzheimer's Research Center (18 whole cerebrums and 58 hemispheres).
evidence: The claim describes the dataset composition.

claim: The MADRC surface scans were acquired using a turntable with an Einscan Pro HD scanner with 0.05 mm point accuracy.
source: The surface scans were acquired using a turntable with an Einscan Pro HD scanner (Shining 3D, Hangzhou, China, 0.05 mm point accuracy).
evidence: The claim describes the acquisition method.

claim: MADRC slices with variable thickness were cut with a dissecting knife on a predefined set of landmarks.
source: Slices with variable thickness were cut with a dissecting knife on a predeﬁned set of landmarks and photographed with a 15.1 MP Canon EOS 50D Digital SLR camera.
evidence: The claim describes the dissection method.

claim: MADRC slices were photographed with a 15.1 MP Canon EOS 50D Digital SLR camera.
source: Slices with variable thickness were cut with a dissecting knife on a predeﬁned set of landmarks and photographed with a 15.1 MP Canon EOS 50D Digital SLR camera.
evidence: The claim describes the photography equipment.

claim: The UW-ADRC dataset includes dissection photography of fixed tissue and companion ex vivo MRI scans for 24 cases.
source: Dissection photography of ﬁxed tissue and companion ex vivo MRI scans for 24 cases (all of them with both hemispheres) from the Alzheimer's Disease Research Center at the University of Washington.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset composition.

claim: All UW-ADRC cases include both hemispheres.
source: Dissection photography of ﬁxed tissue and companion ex vivo MRI scans for 24 cases (all of them with both hemispheres) from the Alzheimer's Disease Research Center at the University of Washington.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset composition.

claim: The UW-ADRC MRI scans were acquired at 0.8 mm isotropic resolution using a FLAIR sequence.
source: The MRI scans were acquired at 0.8 mm isotropic resolution using a FLAIR sequence.
evidence: The claim describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: UW-ADRC coronal slices were cut with 4 mm thickness using a modified deli slicer.
source: Coronal slices were cut with 4 mm thickness using a modiﬁed deli slicer and photographed with a 35 Megapixel (MP) camera.
evidence: The claim describes the dissection method.

claim: UW-ADRC slices were photographed with a 35 Megapixel camera.
source: Coronal slices were cut with 4 mm thickness using a modiﬁed deli slicer and photographed with a 35 Megapixel (MP) camera.
evidence: The claim describes the photography equipment.

claim: No 3D surface scanning was available for the UW-ADRC dataset.
source: While no 3D surface scanning was available for this dataset, we obtained surfaces by skull stripping the MRI scans and meshing the brain surface.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the dataset.

claim: For UW-ADRC, surfaces were obtained by skull stripping the MRI scans and meshing the brain surface.
source: While no 3D surface scanning was available for this dataset, we obtained surfaces by skull stripping the MRI scans and meshing the brain surface.
evidence: The claim describes the method for obtaining surfaces.

claim: Two experienced labelers manually traced the contour of nine brain regions in one slice per case for UW-ADRC.
source: Furthermore, two experienced labelers manually traced the contour of nine brain regions (white matter, cortex, lateral ventricle, thalamus, caudate, putamen, pallidum, hippocampus, and amygdala) in one slice per case, which enables computation of 2D Dice scores.
evidence: The claim describes the manual annotation process.

claim: The HCP dataset includes T1- and T2-weighted MRI scans of 500 subjects acquired at 0.7 mm isotropic resolution.
source: T1- and T2-weighted MRI scans of 500 subjects from the Human Connectome Project, acquired at 0.7 mm isotropic resolution.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset.

claim: The HCP scans were skull stripped using FreeSurfer.
source: The scans were skull stripped using FreeSurfer (Fischl, 2012).
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing method and cites the tool.

claim: The T1-39 dataset comprises 39 T1-weighted MRI scans at 1 mm isotropic resolution with manual volumetric segmentations for 36 brain structures.
source: 39 T1-weighted MRI scans at 1 mm isotropic resolution, with manual volumetric segmentations for 36 brain structures, which we used to train Photo-SynthSeg.
evidence: The claim describes the training dataset.

claim: The T1-39 dataset is the labeled dataset that was used to build the probabilistic atlas in FreeSurfer.
source: We note that this is the labeled dataset that was used to build the probabilistic atlas in FreeSurfer (Fischl et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim describes the origin of the dataset and cites the relevant paper.

claim: The 36 structures in T1-39 include 22 that are segmented by Photo-SynthSeg.
source: The 36 structures include 22 that are segmented by Photo-Synthseg: left and right white matter, cortex, ventricle, thalamus, caudate, putamen, pallidum, hippocampus, amygdala, accumbens area, and ventral diencephalon.
evidence: The claim describes the structures included in the dataset.

claim: Surface scanning is a technology that is becoming increasingly inexpensive, mainly via structured light technology.
source: Surface scanning (also known as 'proﬁlometry') is a technology that is becoming increasingly inexpensive (a few thousand dollars), mainly via structured light technology (Salvi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is stated as a trend in the field and cites relevant work.

claim: The preferred version of the pipeline relies on a surface scan of the specimen acquired before slicing.
source: The preferred version of our proposed pipeline relies on a surface scan of the specimen (Figure 1a) acquired before slicing.
evidence: The claim describes the preferred workflow.

claim: Minimizing geometric distortion between scanning and subsequent slicing is crucial.
source: While there are no speciﬁc technical requirements for the surface scan (e.g., minimum resolution), minimizing geometric distortion (i.e., deformation) between scanning and subsequent slicing is crucial.
evidence: The claim is stated as an important consideration.

claim: The pipeline does not strictly require the surface scan, as it can be replaced with a probabilistic atlas with a slight loss of accuracy.
source: As mentioned earlier, our pipeline does not strictly require the surface scan, as it can be replaced with a probabilistic atlas with a slight loss of accuracy (as shown in the Results section).
evidence: The claim describes an alternative mode and references results.

claim: The pipeline assumes that approximately parallel slices are cut in coronal direction.
source: Speciﬁcally, our pipeline assumes that approximately parallel slices are cut in coronal direction – which is the standard practice in most brain banks.
evidence: The claim describes an assumption of the method.

claim: The pipeline assumes that the thickness of slices is approximately constant.
source: We further assume that the thickness of these slices is approximately constant, as 'thickness jitter' has a detrimental eﬀect on the results (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim describes an assumption and references supporting results.

claim: The pipeline requires the presence of fiducials to enable pixel size calibration and perspective correction.
source: Moreover, we require the presence of ﬁducials to enable pixel size calibration and perspective correction.
evidence: The claim describes a requirement of the method.

claim: Ideally, four fiducials are placed on the corners of a rectangle of known dimensions.
source: Ideally, four ﬁducials are placed on the corners of a rectangle of known dimensions (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim describes the ideal setup and references a figure.

claim: In the absence of fiducials, the pipeline requires the presence of at least a ruler or two orthogonal rulers.
source: In the absence of such ﬁducials, we require the presence of at least a ruler or two orthogonal rulers; the former enables pixel size calibration via image scaling, whereas the latter enables approximate perspective correction by ﬁtting an aﬃne transform.
evidence: The claim describes alternative requirements.

claim: The pipeline allows for multiple slices to be present in one photograph.
source: Our pipeline allows for multiple slices to be present in one photograph but requires that all photographs are of the same side of the slices (either anterior or posterior) and that the inferior–superior direction of the anatomy is approximately aligned with the vertical axis of the image (as in Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim describes a capability of the method.

claim: The pipeline requires that all photographs are of the same side of the slices.
source: Our pipeline allows for multiple slices to be present in one photograph but requires that all photographs are of the same side of the slices (either anterior or posterior) and that the inferior–superior direction of the anatomy is approximately aligned with the vertical axis of the image (as in Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim describes a requirement of the method.

claim: The pipeline requires that the inferior–superior direction of the anatomy is approximately aligned with the vertical axis of the image.
source: Our pipeline allows for multiple slices to be present in one photograph but requires that all photographs are of the same side of the slices (either anterior or posterior) and that the inferior–superior direction of the anatomy is approximately aligned with the vertical axis of the image (as in Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim describes a requirement of the method.

claim: Ideally, the slices should be photographed on a flat board with a solid background color that stands out from the brain tissue.
source: Ideally, the slices should be photographed on a ﬂat board with a solid background color that stands out from the brain tissue, as stronger contrast between tissue and background greatly facilitates image segmentation when preprocessing the photographs (further details below).
evidence: The claim describes an ideal setup and provides reasoning.

claim: SIFT is used to detect fiducials and compute a spatial transform that corrects for perspective distortion and calibrates the pixel size.
source: In the ideal scenario with four ﬁducials, the widespread widespread scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT, Lowe, 1999) is used to detect such ﬁducials (Figure 5b) and compute a spatial transform that corrects for perspective distortion and calibrates the pixel size – see Figure 5c, where the pixel size calibration enables superimposition of a digital ruler.
evidence: The claim describes the method and cites SIFT.

claim: The software supports a manual mode where the user clicks on two, three, or four landmarks.
source: Our software also supports a manual mode where the user clicks on two, three, or four landmarks: two points with a known distance in between (enables approximate pixel size calibration); three points at the ends of two rulers plus their intersection (enables approximate perspective correction with an aﬃne transform); or four points on the corners of a rectangle of known dimensions (enables full perspective correction).
evidence: The claim describes a feature of the software.

claim: After geometric correction, the methods require a binary segmentation of the brain tissue, separating it from the background.
source: After geometric correction, our methods require a binary segmentation of the brain tissue, separating it from the background.
evidence: The claim describes a preprocessing step.

claim: Using a solid background with a distinct color can greatly facilitate segmentation.
source: While our tools do not have any speciﬁc requisites in terms of background, using a solid background with a distinct color (e.g., a 'green screen') can greatly facilitate segmentation; otherwise, more extensive manual intervention may be needed.
evidence: The claim provides practical advice based on experience.

claim: Using a flat black background enabled automatic segmentation of tissue with a combination of thresholding and morphological operations, keeping manual edits to a minimum.
source: In our experiments, using a ﬂat black background enabled us to automatically segment the tissue with a combination of thresholding and morphological operations, keeping manual edits to a minimum (a couple of minutes per photograph, mostly to erase bits of cortical surface that are sometimes visible around the edge of the face of the slice).
evidence: The claim describes the experience with the datasets.

claim: The final preprocessing step requires the user to specify the order of the slices within the photograph.
source: Given this binary mask, the ﬁnal preprocessing step requires the user to specify the order of the slices within the photograph – which may be anterior to posterior or vice versa, but must be consistent within and across photographs of the same case.
evidence: The claim describes a preprocessing requirement.

claim: The user needs to specify whether two connected components belong to the same slice.
source: Moreover, the user also needs to specify whether two connected components belong to the same slice, which often happens around the temporal pole.
evidence: The claim describes a preprocessing requirement.

claim: 3D reconstruction is posed as a joint optimization problem.
source: We pose 3D reconstruction as a joint optimization problem (Pichat et al., 2018; Mancini et al., 2019) and use a 3D reference volume for the registration.
evidence: The claim describes the technical approach and cites relevant work.

claim: The 3D reference volume is ideally a binary 3D mask obtained by rasterizing the triangular mesh from the surface scan.
source: This volume is ideally a binary 3D mask obtained by rasterizing (ﬁlling) the triangular mesh from the surface scan.
evidence: The claim describes the ideal reference.

claim: If a surface scan is not available, one can use a probabilistic atlas of brain shape as a reference.
source: If a surface scan is not available, one can instead use a probabilistic atlas (Shattuck et al., 2008) of brain shape, which provides a rough reference for the reconstruction.
evidence: The claim describes an alternative approach and cites relevant work.

claim: The probabilistic atlas cannot drive the reconstruction toward the actual shape of the specimen nor correct deviations from the user-provided slice thickness.
source: However, this reference cannot drive the reconstruction toward the actual shape of the specimen nor correct deviations from the user-provided slice thickness.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of using the probabilistic atlas.

claim: Affine transforms are required for the photographs due to imperfections in the image preprocessing.
source: We note that aﬃne transforms (rather than rigid) are required for the photographs due to imperfections in the image preprocessing of the previous section; nevertheless, we expect the shear and scaling of these transforms to be small.
evidence: The claim explains the choice of transformation model.

claim: Affine rather than nonlinear transforms are used because the latter compromise the robustness of the registration.
source: Furthermore, we use aﬃne rather than nonlinear transforms because the latter compromise the robustness of the registration, as they introduce huge ambiguity in the space of solutions (e.g., one could add an identical small nonlinear deformation to every slice almost without changing the feature of the 3D reconstruction).
evidence: The claim explains the choice of transformation model with reasoning.

claim: The affine model makes it particularly important to place connected components of the same slice in a correct relative position.
source: This aﬃne model makes it particularly important to place connected components of the same slice in a correct relative position when there is more than one, for example, in the temporal pole.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the implications of the model choice.

claim: The 3D reconstruction is in practice not very sensitive to the exact value of the parameters.
source: Either way, the 3D reconstruction is in practice not very sensitive to the exact value of these parameters.
evidence: The claim is an observation about the robustness of the method.

claim: SIFT is not a good candidate for matching consecutive slices because it is not robust against changes in the object itself.
source: We also note that, as opposed to the preprocessing described in the previous section, SIFT is not a good candidate for matching consecutive slices: while it is resilient against changes in pose (e.g., object rotation), perspective, and lightning, it is not robust against changes in the object itself – such as changes between one slice to the next.
evidence: The claim explains why SIFT is not used for slice matching.

claim: The LBFGS optimizer is initialized by stacking the photographs with their centers of gravity on coordinate (0,0), and then matching the center of gravity of the whole stack with the center of gravity of the 3D reference.
source: The LBFGS optimizer is initialized by stacking the photographs with their centers of gravity on coordinate (0,0), and then matching the center of gravity of the whole stack with the center of gravity of the 3D reference (as illustrated in Video 1 in the supplement, see also https://youtu.be/wo5meYRaGUY).
evidence: The claim describes the initialization procedure.

claim: The probabilistic atlas produces a plausible reconstruction, which is however far from the real shape of the specimen given by the surface.
source: The probabilistic atlas produces a plausible reconstruction, which is however far from the real shape of the specimen given by the surface (Figure 5g).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison in Figure 5g.

claim: 3D reconstruction is implemented in PyTorch and runs efficiently on a GPU in less than 5 minutes.
source: We note that 3D reconstruction is implemented in PyTorch, and runs eﬃciently on a GPU – less than 5 min on a Nvidia Quadro RTX 6000.
evidence: The claim describes the implementation and performance.

claim: There are two main challenges when segmenting 3D reconstructed photographs: varying appearance across cases and estimating segmentation in between slices.
source: There are two main challenges when segmenting the 3D reconstructed photographs. First, the appearance of the images varies widely across cases due to diﬀerences in camera hardware (sensor, lens), camera settings, illumination conditions, and tissue preparation (e.g., ﬁxed vs fresh). And second, accurate volumetry requires estimating the segmentation not only on the planes of the photographs but also in between slices.
evidence: The claim describes the challenges addressed by the method.

claim: The previous work adopted a Bayesian segmentation strategy that handled appearance variation but not interpolation between slices.
source: In our previous work (Tregidgo et al., 2020), we adopted a Bayesian segmentation strategy that handled the ﬁrst issue but not the second.
evidence: The claim describes limitations of prior work, citing it.

claim: Photo-SynthSeg extends a machine learning approach based on domain randomization that was successfully applied to segment clinical brain MRI scans with large slice spacing.
source: Here, we extend a machine learning approach based on domain randomization (Tobin et al., 2017) that we have successfully applied to segment clinical brain MRI scans with large slice spacing (Billot et al., 2020; Billot et al., 2023a; Billot et al., 2023b).
evidence: The claim describes the approach and cites relevant prior work.

claim: Photo-SynthSeg trains a 3D U-Net with synthetic data.
source: Speciﬁcally, our newly proposed approach 'Photo-SynthSeg' trains a convolutional neural network for image segmentation (a 3D U-Net, Ronneberger et al., 2015; Çiçek et al., 2019) with synthetic data as follows.
evidence: The claim describes the method and cites the U-Net architecture.

claim: Photo-SynthSeg starts from a training dataset that comprises a pool of 3D segmentations of brain images at isotropic 3D resolution.
source: 'Photo-SynthSeg' starts from a training dataset (the T1-39 dataset) that comprises a pool of 3D segmentations of brain images at isotropic 3D resolution (Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim describes the training data.

claim: At every iteration during training, one 3D segmentation is randomly selected and geometrically deformed with a random nonlinear transform.
source: At every iteration during training, one of these 3D segmentations is randomly selected and geometrically deformed with a random nonlinear transform, which simulates imperfect 3D reconstruction by including a 'deformation jitter' in the coronal direction, that is, small but abrupt deformations from one coronal slice to the next (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim describes the training procedure.

claim: The deformed isotropic segmentation is used to generate a synthetic 3D image using a Gaussian mixture model conditioned on the segmentation.
source: This deformed isotropic segmentation is used to generate a synthetic 3D image (also at isotropic resolution) using a Gaussian mixture model conditioned on the segmentation (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim describes the image synthesis process.

claim: The Gaussian parameters (means and variances) are randomized to make the neural network robust against variations in image appearance.
source: Crucially, we randomize the Gaussian parameters (means and variances) to make the neural network robust against variations in image appearance.
evidence: The claim describes a key aspect of the training strategy.

claim: The synthetic isotropic image is digitally sliced into a 3D stack of synthetic coronal photographs, each corrupted by a random 2D smooth illumination field.
source: This synthetic isotropic image is then 'digitally sliced' into a 3D stack of synthetic coronal photographs, each of which is independently corrupted by a random 2D smooth illumination ﬁeld that simulates inhomogeneities in the illumination of the photographs (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim describes the simulation of photographic artifacts.

claim: The thickness of the simulated slices is randomized in every iteration.
source: Importantly, we also randomize the thickness of the simulated slices in every iteration and introduce small stochastic variations in thickness around the central value within each simulation.
evidence: The claim describes the domain randomization strategy.

claim: Randomizing slice thickness makes the network agnostic to the slice thickness of the reconstructed 3D stack at test time.
source: This strategy makes the network agnostic to the slice thickness of the reconstructed 3D stack at test time.
evidence: The claim explains the purpose of thickness randomization.

claim: The simulated stack is resampled to the original isotropic resolution of the deformed 3D segmentation.
source: Finally, the simulated stack, which has anisotropic resolution (e.g., 1 mm in-plane and several mm in slice thickness), is resampled to the original isotropic resolution of the (deformed) 3D segmentation (Figure 6e) – typically 1 mm isotropic.
evidence: The claim describes the final step of data preparation.

claim: Photo-SynthSeg is a U-Net that will produce a high-resolution (1 mm) isotropic 3D segmentation for every input at test time, independently of the slice spacing.
source: This generative process mimics the image formation process in the real world and has two crucial aspects. First, the super-resolution component: Photo-SynthSeg is a U-Net that will produce a high-resolution (1 mm) isotropic 3D segmentation for every input at test time, independently of the slice spacing of the 3D reconstructed stack of photographs (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim describes a key capability of the method.

claim: Domain randomization forces the U-Net to learn features that are independent of the intensity profiles of the photographs and of the spacing between slices.
source: And second, domain randomization: sampling diﬀerent Gaussian parameters, illumination ﬁelds, and slice thicknesses at every iteration beyond realistic limits (as in Figure 6, where even contralateral regions have diﬀerent appearance) forces the U-Net to learn features that are independent of the intensity proﬁles of the photographs, as well as of the spacing between slices.
evidence: The claim explains the mechanism of domain randomization.

claim: Domain randomization makes the U-Net robust against changes in the acquisition.
source: This process makes the U-Net robust against changes in the acquisition.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the effect of domain randomization.

claim: The Gaussian distributions are univariate rather than trivariate, modeling grayscale rather than RGB triplets.
source: We note that the Gaussian distributions are univariate rather than trivariate, that is, they model grayscale rather than red–green–blue triplets; we tried training a U-Net with the latter, but the performance on color images was worse than when converting them to grayscale and using the U-Net trained with univariate Gaussians.
evidence: The claim describes a design choice and provides empirical justification.

claim: The U-Net architecture consists of five levels, each separated by a batch normalization layer along with a max-pooling or upsampling operation.
source: The U-Net architecture is the same as in our previous works with synthetic scans (Billot et al., 2020; Billot et al., 2023a): it consists of ﬁve levels, each separated by a batch normalization layer (Ioﬀe and Szegedy, 2015) along with a max-pooling (contracting path) or an upsampling operation (expanding path).
evidence: The claim describes the network architecture and cites relevant work.

claim: All levels comprise two convolution layers with 3 × 3 × 3 kernels.
source: All levels comprise two convolution layers with 3 × 3 × 3 kernels.
evidence: The claim describes the network architecture.

claim: Every convolutional layer is associated with an Exponential Linear Unit activation, except for the last one, which uses a softmax.
source: Every convolutional layer is associated with an Exponential Linear Unit activation (Clevert et al., 2016), except for the last one, which uses a softmax.
evidence: The claim describes the network architecture and cites the activation function.

claim: The first layer comprises 24 feature maps, and this number is doubled after each max-pooling and halved after each upsampling.
source: While the ﬁrst layer comprises 24 feature maps, this number is doubled after each max-pooling, and halved after each upsampling.
evidence: The claim describes the network architecture.

claim: Skip connections are used across the contracting and expanding paths.
source: Following the original U-Net architecture, skip connections are used across the contracting and expanding paths.
evidence: The claim describes the network architecture.

claim: The network is trained with a soft Dice loss and the Adam optimizer.
source: The network is trained with a soft Dice loss (Milletari et al., 2016) and the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the training procedure and cites relevant work.

claim: The deep learning model is implemented in Keras with a Tensorflow backend.
source: The deep learning model is implemented in Keras (Chollet, 2015) with a Tensorﬂow backend (Abadi et al., 2016) and runs on a few seconds on a Nvidia Quadro RTX 6000 GPU.
evidence: The claim describes the implementation and cites the frameworks.

claim: The deep learning model runs in a few seconds on a Nvidia Quadro RTX 6000 GPU.
source: The deep learning model is implemented in Keras (Chollet, 2015) with a Tensorﬂow backend (Abadi et al., 2016) and runs on a few seconds on a Nvidia Quadro RTX 6000 GPU.
evidence: The claim describes the computational performance.

claim: Training takes around 7 days on a Nvidia Quadro RTX 6000 GPU.
source: Training takes around 7 days on the same GPU.
evidence: The claim describes the training time.

claim: There are two different versions of Photo-SynthSeg: one for full cerebra and one for single hemispheres.
source: Finally, we note that there are two diﬀerent versions of Photo-SynthSeg: one for full cerebra and one for single hemispheres.
evidence: The claim describes the available versions of the tool.

claim: The hemisphere version is trained with left hemispheres and flipped right hemispheres.
source: The later is trained with left hemispheres and ﬂipped right hemispheres, and can thus be used as is for left hemispheres.
evidence: The claim describes the training approach for the hemisphere version.

claim: To process a right hemisphere, the image is left–right flipped, segmented, and the results are flipped back.
source: To process a right hemisphere, we simply left–right ﬂip it, segment it, and ﬂip the results back.
evidence: The claim describes the processing procedure for right hemispheres.

claim: The default Photo-SynthSeg pipeline segments the cerebral cortex as a whole.
source: While the default Photo-SynthSeg pipeline segments the cerebral cortex as a whole (i.e., as in Figure 6a), our tool also oﬀers the option of subdividing it into parcels as deﬁned by the Desikan–Killiany atlas (Desikan et al., 2009), like in Figure 2.
evidence: The claim describes the default behavior of the tool.

claim: Photo-SynthSeg offers the option of subdividing the cortex into parcels as defined by the Desikan–Killiany atlas.
source: While the default Photo-SynthSeg pipeline segments the cerebral cortex as a whole (i.e., as in Figure 6a), our tool also oﬀers the option of subdividing it into parcels as deﬁned by the Desikan–Killiany atlas (Desikan et al., 2009), like in Figure 2.
evidence: The claim describes an optional feature and cites the atlas.

claim: Cortical parcellation is achieved with the cortical parcellation module (Segmenter S3) of SynthSeg.
source: This is achieved with the cortical parcellation module (Segmenter S3) of our tool 'SynthSeg' (Billot et al., 2023a), which is also distributed with FreeSurfer.
evidence: The claim describes the implementation and cites the tool.
